title: WHEN SOMEONE WANTS ACCESS TO YOUR BODY BUT NOT RESPONSIBILITY FOR YOUR LIFE
paragraphs: WHEN SOMEONE WANTS ACCESS TO YOUR BODY BUT NOT RESPONSIBILITY FOR YOUR LIFE

They may call it love. They may say, “Why do we need a label?” They may want your touch, your loyalty, your vulnerability, your late-night conversations—and still refuse the covenant, responsibility, holiness, and sacrifice that biblical love requires. Before you give someone what God calls sacred, ask yourself one painful question: Do they actually want to love me… or do they only want access to me?
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that does not begin when someone leaves.
It begins while they are still there.
Still texting.
Still calling.
Still saying they miss you.
Still wanting to come over.
Still reaching for your body.
Still expecting your emotional availability.
Still becoming jealous when someone else gets your attention.
Still wanting privileges that feel suspiciously like commitment...
while carefully avoiding the responsibility of actually committing.
And perhaps that is why this hurts so much.
Because sometimes the person who is using you does not look cruel.
Sometimes they are affectionate.
Sometimes they are wounded too.
Sometimes they know exactly what to say when you begin pulling away.
“I care about you.”
“I’m just not ready.”
“Why do we have to complicate this?”
“Can’t we just enjoy what we have?”
Maybe you have heard those words.
Maybe you have said them.
Maybe you are living inside them right now.
And somewhere beneath all the chemistry, loneliness, hope, excuses, physical desire, and spiritual conviction, there is a question you have been afraid to ask:
If this person wants access to my body but refuses responsibility for my life, is this actually love?
Scripture gives us a far deeper vision of intimacy than our culture does.
Go all the way back to Genesis.
Before dating apps.
Before hookup culture.
Before pornography became available through a screen.
Before situationships had a name.
Before human beings learned a thousand sophisticated ways to separate sexual intimacy from covenantal responsibility, Scripture said:
“עַל־כֵּן֙ יַֽעֲזָב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד׃”
Genesis 2:24.
A careful translation is:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Notice the movement.
Leave.
Hold fast.
Become one flesh.
The Hebrew verb וְדָבַק — wəḏāḇaq, from dāḇaq — carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, remaining closely joined.
That matters.
Because the biblical vision does not begin with:
Take what you want.
Enjoy the body.
Avoid responsibility.
Keep your options open.
Disappear when things become inconvenient.
God's design places “one flesh” inside a relationship marked by a profound joining of lives.
Jesus Himself later reaches back to this very passage when teaching about marriage.
That means your body is not spiritually meaningless.
Sex is not merely recreation performed by consenting bodies.
Biblically, sexual union possesses a seriousness our culture desperately tries to make casual.
And casual sex often discovers too late that the body participated in something the heart cannot casually forget.
Paul understood that.
Writing to Corinth—a world hardly unfamiliar with sexual disorder—he did not treat the body as disposable packaging around the “real” spiritual person.
He wrote:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not keep it around until you become spiritually stronger.
Not see how close you can get without crossing whatever line you have drawn.
Flee.
Then Paul says something astonishing.
“τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς... ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν”
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
And then:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς”
“You were bought with a price.”
Therefore:
“δοξάσατε... τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι”
Glorify God in your body.
That changes the question completely.
The question is no longer merely:
“Do I want this person?”
Or:
“Does this person want me?”
The deeper question becomes:
“Does what we are doing glorify the Christ who purchased me?”
Because Christian sexual ethics are not fundamentally about God hating pleasure.
They are about belonging.
You belong to Christ.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your sexuality belongs under the lordship of Christ.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Christ.
Your loneliness belongs under the lordship of Christ.
Even that aching part of you that desperately wants someone to choose you belongs to Jesus.
And perhaps this is where the truth gets uncomfortable.
Sometimes we do not surrender our bodies because we are overwhelmed by lust.
Sometimes we surrender them because we are terrified of being abandoned.
Sometimes what looks like sexual temptation is actually loneliness wearing different clothes.
You were afraid that saying no would make them leave.
You were afraid boundaries would make you seem difficult.
Old-fashioned.
Religious.
Boring.
Unlovable.
So you compromised a little.
Then another little.
Then another.
And every compromise came with a promise whispered somewhere inside:
Maybe now they will choose me.
Maybe now they will stay.
Maybe now I will finally be enough.
But they kept taking pieces of intimacy while withholding the security your heart was begging for.
And slowly you began negotiating against yourself.
You called anxiety “butterflies.”
You called inconsistency “complicated.”
You called secrecy “privacy.”
You called sexual pressure “passion.”
You called crumbs “love” because you were starving.
Please hear this carefully.
This article is not telling you that every person who struggles sexually is an evil predator.
Christians must be more truthful and more compassionate than that.
Two people can genuinely care about each other and still participate together in something sinful.
Two wounded people can exploit one another without initially understanding the depth of what they are doing.
A boyfriend or girlfriend can feel genuine affection and still pressure the other sexually.
A person can sincerely believe they love you while behaving in ways that are selfish, immature, manipulative, or unholy.
And sometimes...
you may be the one demanding access.
You may be the person pushing boundaries.
You may be the one saying, “If you really loved me...”
You may be the one keeping somebody emotionally attached because you enjoy what they provide while secretly knowing you have no intention of offering faithful commitment.
The Gospel does not permit us to read articles like this only looking for somebody else's sin.
The Word is a mirror.
So before you send this to the person who hurt you, allow God to search you too.
Paul's words to the Thessalonians become especially piercing here:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν”
“This is the will of God: your sanctification.”
He continues by commanding believers to abstain from porneia—sexual immorality—and to live in holiness and honor.
Then, in the same discussion, Paul warns against transgressing against and exploiting another person in this matter.
Do you see how radical that is?
Biblical sexual holiness is not simply:
“Don't have sex.”
It asks what you are doing with another human being who bears God's image.
Are you honoring them?
Are you exploiting them?
Are you awakening intimacy while refusing responsibility?
Are you manipulating their fear of losing you?
Are you encouraging them toward Christ—or teaching them that keeping you requires compromising Him?
That question can expose an entire relationship.
Because someone who genuinely loves you should not require your disobedience to God as proof of your devotion to them.
Read that again.
Someone who genuinely loves you should not require your disobedience to God as proof of your devotion to them.
“I need this.”
“Everybody does it.”
“We're going to get married eventually.”
“God knows we love each other.”
“You're being too religious.”
“If you trusted me, you would.”
No.
Love does not need to drag you away from Jesus to prove that it exists.
Love should want your holiness more than it wants immediate gratification.
That does not mean a godly relationship will be free from temptation.
Quite the opposite.
Two people can deeply love Christ and still experience powerful sexual desire for each other.
Attraction is not automatically sin.
Temptation is not automatically defeat.
Desire itself does not make you filthy.
But love learns restraint because love sees another person's soul as more valuable than tonight's satisfaction.
Lust asks:
“How much can I get?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor you before God?”
Lust wants access.
Love accepts responsibility.
Lust consumes.
Love protects.
Lust becomes angry when boundaries interfere with gratification.
Love can hear “no” without punishing you for it.
And Christian love understands something else.
Marriage is not merely a license for sex.
Marriage is covenantal self-giving.
Scripture's picture of marriage eventually reaches its highest theological horizon in Christ and His Church.
Ephesians 5 does not tell husbands merely to desire their wives.
It tells husbands to love their wives “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Look at Jesus.
That is our standard.
Christ does not exploit His Bride.
He gives Himself for her.
Christ does not say:
Give Me everything while I remain accountable for nothing.
He lays Himself down.
Christian love therefore cannot be defined merely by intensity of desire.
Sacrificial love asks what it costs me to seek the good of the person I claim to love.
And maybe right now your heart is breaking because you realize:
They wanted the benefits of closeness without the weight of covenant.
They wanted your nakedness without your future.
Your affection without accountability.
Your loyalty without commitment.
Your body without the responsibility of protecting your heart.
But before anger consumes you, remember something even more important.
Your worth is not determined by whether that person finally chooses you.
Jesus already moved toward sinners at unimaginable cost.
At the cross, Christ did not merely tell you that you were loved.
He demonstrated holy, sacrificial love.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He gave Himself.
He rose again.
And He calls sinners—not merely sexually broken sinners, but all sinners—to repentance, forgiveness, cleansing, and new life.
Which means there is another person reading this article.
Not the person wondering whether to leave a compromising relationship.
The person who already crossed the line.
Again.
And again.
Maybe you slept with someone you were never married to.
Maybe you moved from relationship to relationship trying to make intimacy cure loneliness.
Maybe you have been sexually used.
Maybe you used somebody.
Maybe pornography taught you to see bodies as commodities.
Maybe you have lived with someone for years while continually postponing obedience.
Maybe you knew exactly what Scripture said...
and did the opposite.
And now shame is whispering:
This article is proof that God is disgusted with you.
No.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not call sin righteousness.
But neither does Jesus tell repentant sinners that their sin is stronger than His grace.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her sexual sin was exposed publicly.
Humiliation surrounded her.
Accusers were ready.
And Jesus did something neither cheap grace nor religious cruelty knows how to do.
He refused to condemn her...
and He refused to redefine her sin.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
Then:
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Grace and repentance stood in the same conversation.
That is Jesus.
He does not say your sexual past does not matter.
He says it does not have to own your future.
He does not save you so you can make peace with chains.
He saves you and calls you out of them.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the sinner finally stopping long enough to admit:
Jesus, my way is killing me.
I want Yours.
Maybe your repentance means ending a sexual relationship.
Maybe it means confessing what you have hidden.
Maybe it means telling the person you love:
“I love you too much to keep helping both of us disobey Jesus.”
Maybe it means moving out.
Maybe it means establishing boundaries you should have established months ago.
Maybe it means seeking wise pastoral counsel and Christian accountability.
Maybe it means blocking the number that becomes irresistible after midnight.
Maybe it means deleting what continually pulls you back.
Maybe it means admitting that the relationship you keep calling complicated is actually keeping you spiritually compromised.
And sometimes repentance means admitting something even harder:
You cannot heal someone by giving them unlimited access to you.
You cannot make an unwilling person covenant-minded by becoming more sexually available.
You cannot turn lust into love by giving lust everything it asks for.
You cannot purchase commitment with your body.
And you should never have to audition physically for a role that requires covenantal faithfulness.
But there is an equally important warning here.
Do not transform biblical boundaries into pride.
Do not walk away saying:
“I am pure. They are disgusting.”
Without Christ, none of us stands righteous before God.
Sexual purity does not save you.
Virginity does not save you.
Marriage does not save you.
Your ability to maintain boundaries does not save you.
Jesus saves sinners.
And some of the most beautifully restored followers of Christ have histories they once believed disqualified them forever.
The scandal of grace is that Jesus receives repentant people whose stories make religious crowds uncomfortable.
The woman with the reputation.
The adulterer.
The porn addict.
The person who sold intimacy for affection.
The person who destroyed a marriage.
The person who thought their body was the only thing they had to offer.
The person who knew better.
The person who should have stopped.
The person who didn't.
The person whose scandal became public.
The person whose scandal remains hidden.
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you wish you could tear out.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Then let Him teach you how to walk differently.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture outrage.
Not to make wounded people hate the people who wounded them.
Not to create a Christian version of relationship revenge.
We want people to encounter Jesus Christ—the Savior who speaks truth strong enough to expose sin and offers grace deep enough to redeem sinners.
If this article exposed something hidden in you, don't rush past that conviction.
Talk to Jesus.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It doesn't.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes bringing into the light what you have spent years hiding is the first public crack in a prison door.
And if you have been pretending everything is fine while privately falling apart:
“No more hiding.”
There are people reading the comments who need to discover they are not the only Christian who has struggled.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
But if this message is faithful to Scripture and you believe somebody needs it, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.
Send it privately to the friend who keeps returning to the person who keeps breaking them.
Send it to the Christian couple quietly compromising while convincing themselves that eventually they will fix everything.
Send it to the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely sexual prohibition and has never heard that Christian holiness flows from belonging to Christ.
Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God's blessing. You cannot buy His favor.
But you can choose to support work that you believe helps spread biblical truth.
Stay close because you want to grow.
Stay because you want Scripture when your emotions become louder than truth.
Stay because discipleship requires more than occasionally encountering a Christian post while scrolling.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who knows something inside has gone cold.
Even invite the unbeliever who has questions about Jesus.
Because loneliness has a strange way of making yesterday's conviction difficult to remember tonight.
There may come a night when the phone lights up.
Their name appears.
Your heart races.
And suddenly everything you knew while reading this feels negotiable.
Come back.
Read it again.
Remember who purchased you.
Remember:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.”
You were bought with a price.
Your body is not bargaining currency for affection.
Your boundaries are not cruelty.
Your obedience is not prudishness.
And losing someone because you chose faithfulness to Christ is not the same thing as losing everything.
If following Jesus costs you a relationship that required you to keep disobeying Jesus in order to preserve it...
you have not lost your Savior.
You still have Christ.
And Christ is enough to begin again.
Not to prove you love God.
Not to purchase His blessing.
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
They may simply read.
Cry.
Close the door they should have closed months ago.
Fall beside their bed.
And whisper:
“Jesus... I choose You.”
And perhaps that will be the moment the story changes.
Because the final word over a surrendered life does not belong to the person who used you.
It does not belong to the person who abandoned you.
It does not belong to your sexual history.
It does not belong to shame.
It does not belong to the night you wish you could undo.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
And when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered story, even the chapter that made you think everything was ruined can become the place where grace began rewriting everything.
Never trade the arms of Christ for the arms of someone who needs you to walk away from Christ to keep holding them.
